blocks.x: Walter "Foots" Thomas/Milt Hinton (January 5, 1981):
This is January 5th, 1981, and I am sitting here with my dear friend, Walter P. Thomas. What's that "p" for, Foots?
What do you always call me, Walter Pearl?
Right, yeah! Walter Pearl Thomas. He's nicknamed Foots Thomas...
Looks like I'll never live that down.

Well, no, that's your (?), Foots. That's you. I'm talking to you for the Smithsonian Institute, because the world should know about you and the contributions, the tremendous contributions that you've given to music.

So let's start from the beginning, Foots. When were you born?
I was born February the Tenth, 1907. And to put it in the right perspective, I was born a month and teen days after Oklahoma went into statehood.
Wow. What town?

Muskogee, Oklahoma. And they had a deal before statehood that every child that was born in Oklahoma was given 150 acres of land. They did that to influence people to come and settle in Oklahoma. I'll tell you later about my grandfather, because he came over earlier. And...
Thomas - 2

I was the first child born in Oklahoma. My other brother and sister, George and Cleora, they were born in Texas. And that had a great effect on my life, as I later analyzed it. I don't know what I was doing, analyzing things that young. But I went to a grade school...
Well, before you go into grade school, Foots, I want to know your father's name and your mother's name.
My father's name was Joseph Thomas. And my mother's name was Magdalen. I'd always known it as Maggie, but it was Magdalen.
They were from Texas?

Yeah, from Texas. My grandfather, I found out later, was Tennessee or Georgia. My daughter is busy in the archives finding out all about my parents. And I don't know whether my mother was born in Texas. But I know that I always thought they all came from Texas. But I found out they migrated from I think it was Georgia -- because my grandmother was part-Indian, you know.
I guess it's a good time to talk about my grandfather.
Sure.

My grandfather... See, Oklahoma opened the territory, and I don't know what year it was; it must have been eighteen-something. And he sold... I understand that my Grandfather was a slave. So his slave-owner gave him and
Thomas - 3

all his dependents, his children, some of the best black-bottom land in Texas. He sold everybody's land, sold his, my mother's and everybody else's, to get money to go to Oklahoma. So the deal was, they drove up to the Oklahoma-Texas border, and they had to stay on the Texas side until twelve o'clock at night.
What was the reason for that?

Well, they had to wait until twelve o'clock, because that was the time to go in, twelve o'clock at night. I don't know the reason. But twelve o'clock at night is when they'd sound the trumpet or shoot the gun or something, and then everybody would go over and homestead.
Oh yeah. I remember hearing about that.

And I ran into some of my relatives down in Texas, Luther Manning, and he told me the story about my grandfather. He said when they...whatever signal they gave to go in... He said my grandmother was sitting on the horse asleep! And boy, the Manning family was a sleeping family. We could sleep anywhere...
What's his name, Manning?
Manning, yeah.
And that was your mother's side?
That was my mother's side. And so he said he was sleeping. And my grandfather was a vagabond. He
Thomas - 4

traveled.... He didn't stay no place no length of time. My grandmother told me this story. One thing about him, he was too religious to take some of that land. They was givin' the land away! Wasn't no (?). They wanted you to come in there and homestead it and use it. It was yours. And he'd have got enough land for his dependents if he'd known. But my grandmother said he was too religious. He thought he was taking something from somebody. And here they was, givin' it away.

And Milt, that one little incident had a lot to do with my life. Because I saw how the different natives had land, and then they didn't have it, and half of them didn't get an education. And that influenced on me to go and learn something so... I didn't have no land. And I guess I can start... The earliest I know is in kindergarten.
Yeah!

Oklahoma is one of the most blessed places I know to be in anywhere in the world. How they influenced all those different people to come in there and settle, it was a mystery to me later on. Now, this kindergarten teacher, she knew a little music. And this kindergarten school was in my section of the town. It was only a block from my house. And all the kids from all over Muskogee came to that school. I mean, we had a reading (?), the south
Thomas - 5
side, a north side and west side -- but everybody came to that one little school. And here I was just one block... one block from it.

I remember the first... She gave us a little song... She gave me a little song to sing when I was a kid when I was a little kid, "I Got A Dog Named Rover." I can't sing it now; I never could sing it. But I sang it then. And when I went to grade school, I guess I was in about the second grade... If I wasn't in second grade, I was advanced in the first grade, because she taught us our ABC's and all that.

So I got up to the fifth grade, and I failed in mathematics. And as young as I was, I said to myself, "I've got to be some kind of nut to not be studying..." I didn't have nothing to do, because... My family didn't have a lot of money, but we didn't have to worry about nothing. All I had to do was go to school and study. And here I was, failing Mathematics. So they was going to put me back in the fifth grade, but they put me over in the sixth grade on condition. And the condition was that if I kept up with the sixth grade, I wouldn't have to go back. And man, that was a break for me. I studied as hard as I ever studied, so I (?)thought I would study more(?). And I was so good in the sixth grade in Math... This may sound funny. I was so good,
Thomas - 6

I didn't have to take the final examination. Because all them tests they had, I thought that was (?) I had to make those tests... Because I got A's and B's in all the tests. And guess who my teacher was.
Who?
Ingrid(?) Jessie. And I didn't meet her until about two or three years ago to thank her for what she did for me.
I think she just passed recently. I haven't seen her.

Well, she came here from Atlanta. She was out at Michigan for a while, and then I think she went to some school in Oklahoma. I haven't heard of her (?). She did a lot of arranging in choral groups for the different shoes.
She was marvelous.
Yes, she was.
The person who introduced her to me... Charlie Banks was...

Yeah, Charlie Banks was the one that told me she was in town. Boy, I rushed up there to see her, because I couldn't wait to thank her. Because she was the one that gave me that foundation that got my mind together. Because when I graduated in that sixth grade, I think I was at about
Thomas - 7

the head of the class. But that was an influence on me. And I'll tell anybody. If you get sixth grade math, which is fractions, you've got the basics of math. You can figure out anything if you can figure them fractions out.

So when I went... I don't remember too much of the math I had in the seventh and eighth grades in Muskogee. So I talked my mother into letting me go off to school. A buddy of mine had gone to Wilberforce, came back and told me how good it was going off to school. So I found out about this school in Topeka, so I talked my mother into sending me there. My father wanted me to wait a year later. But my mother said, "Don't worry about it. You go on."

So I did. I went and made that... I started almost like you do it in college. I started in my freshman year. And how I got ahold of all them good teachers, I'll never know. I had one woman teacher, one female teacher, and one guy named McCord. He had a knot on his head. And we always thought all that knowledge was up there in that knot. And they were... To me they were so great, because the one thing they told us in the freshman class, he said, "Algebra is only arithmetic in algebraic form." Well, I had my arithmetic, so I flew through that algebra. Then I got to geometry... I think that's when we had the lady teacher. And she told us that geometry was just another phase of
Thomas - 8
arithmetic where you deal with the angles and lines and circles.
I got so crazy about math after my first two years in high school, I took four years of math in high school. And after I finished high school, I had one year of college to my credit.

And I was privileged to be valedictorian, which I didn't know what valedictorian was... But we had an English from Columbia, Mr. Drury. So we had had our first year of Latin in the Freshman class, but we didn't take it no more. And we got up to the Senior Class, and Mr. Drury come and told us that you got to have two years of a foreign language. In those days Latin was a foreign language. Nowadays, They got the Spanish and French and German and all that. So who would go teach us but Mr. Drury?! And Milt, he had to discern that we wondered what was he doing teaching us Latin. Because he was an English teacher! And after about the third or fourth day, he straightened us out. He let us understand that he had studied Latin, German, French and Italian -- he had about six or seven languages! We didn't say nothin' else about it. We let Mr. Drury take charge!
And he was so wonderful to us, because he knew that we didn't remember all that first grade of Latin from the
Thomas - 9
Freshman to the Senior class. And that way, he didn't rush us through, you know. But he told us one thing. He said, "If you get Latin, you'll have English." And it's so true. He was wonderful.
He was right. And all the other languages.

Right. And then another thing that he did for me... Here I am, valedictorian. So evidently, he knew that I didn't know too much about being a valedictorian. At first I didn't know what a valedictorian was. I found later that I was the one that had the highest grade from the Freshman to the Senior class in the same class. Because one boy had higher grades than me, but he had missed one year out, and he came in on our class. But originally, he was supposed to be a class ahead of us. Ralph Waller. So Mr. Drury patiently would sit down with me and helped me write my Valedictorian speech.

Now, he was also our Economics teacher and our Public Speech teacher. These were three of the classes we had a chance to study in high school! And man, that was a privilege, when you think of it. Because some of them... Economics, you don't generally get it until you get to college. And to this day, they taught us things in Economics...
Thomas - 10

And one thing he stressed in Economics, that the Laws of Economics never change. And it bugs me to this day when they're always trying to change it. Because he... I will cite one or two things that have always been important in my mind. The one thing he brought out, he says, "salaries will never keep up with prices." And then you know that one law in Economics, demand and supply. If there's plenty of it, it's cheaper; if there is little of it, it's high. Demand and supply. And those two laws to me ain't never changed. Because look what we've... We don't have no oil, so we've got to buy it from over there. But these new economic leaders come out with some new jazz, and... And evidently, some people have never studied Economics!
And I remember another thing he told us. He said no bank could stand a run.
No what?

No bank could stand a run on a bank. Like if you had your money there and somebody goes around to you and says, "Man, you'd better get your money out of that bank because it's going to fold," and everybody starts to get their money out of that bank -- it's got to fold. And I didn't realize what was wrong with that, because to this day... Because the banks all them other days have been lending out money, so your money ain't there!
Thomas - 11
I know. That's how they make money.
Right. That's... That's where they make their money. Look what they've been doing in the last three or four months or the last year.
They've been (?) the Federal Reserve now.
That's right. And...
Excuse me. Who was this teacher's name?
Mr. Drury. I don't remember his first name. Drury. And he had... One thing I remember, he studied at Columbia. And another thing that he was adamant...
Was he White or Black?
He was Black. All of my teachers were Black. I didn't have no White teachers. We had some light ones, but we didn't have no White ones.

And another thing he taught us... Oh, I started to explain to you about when he first taught us about the banking thing. He said, now, if you want to establish your credit, you go to one bank and you borrow five thousand dollars. And when that note comes due, go to another bank and borrow five thousand dollars to pay that bank off. And once you've paid that bank off, you've established the credit. But it means you've got to go there and pay that other bank off later. And we had one boy in our class, he was going around borrowing, money, but his one problem was,
Thomas - 12

he wasn't payin' back! So he got to the point where he couldn't borrow no money. Because he just heard the one part of it, borrowing money... You know, nothing much, one dollar, five dollars, when you got your allowance.

But Mr. Drury was so smart. And I've always had... The one thing he was adamant about, he wanted us to be able to enter any college in the United States. He said, "If you get the right grades and you have the right classes, you can enter any college in the United States." Because we had an A-program, and he knew it. Now, he was the head of the whole academic thing, so he stressed that with us.

He even taught us Drama! And he taught us just like any Drama teacher. I remember once that I played the part of Dr. Rank in A Doll's House. And he told me something that influenced me later in life. He said a doctor, if he gets complicated, never loses his dignity, and he'll always walk up straight... You won't never see no doctor fallin' all over everybody and stumblin', but he'll always try to use his dignity to stand up straight. He can be drunk... And Dr. Rank was a drunkard, you know. And I had to play this part, so that was for me.
But I remembered all them thing later in life, you know. Because I think teachers are the greatest influence on anybody's life. Because I had one or two teachers...
Thomas - 13
[INAUDIBLE]

Right. Now, guess who my first band teacher was! Man, how I got involved in music... My father wanted me to be an architect. So I went to school, and they had carpentry there, and I figured mechanical drawing, and carpentry was the nearest thing to me getting into architecture, because an architect needs know how to build, what to use as stones and all that. So I studied carpentry with Mr. Burke.
I'm trying to think now how I got involved... Oh. William L. Dawson was our first band teacher .
A good trombone player.
Yeah. He came there. He came right... I think he came right out of Tuskegee.
Now, what was the name of this school you went to?

Kansas Vocational Institute. That was the first name. Then they changed it later, when they added a couple of college studies... They changed it to Kansas Vocational College. Now, it was a state-supported school for Blacks only. The name of the college that was in Topeka was Washburn. And of course, you could go to any of the colleges. But this was a high school set up s a trade school, and it was set up on the way that Tuskegee was.
Thomas - 14

Because we had... I can't remember exactly, but we had four or five teachers from Tuskegee. And I guess that's how we got ahold of Dawson, because when they found out we needed a band teacher, they got him. He was a young teacher down there in Tuskegee...

And do you know, that man influenced me on tone? He had the most gorgeous tone on trombone I had ever heard... Well, I hadn't heard many trombone players anyway. And he kept his trombone shined; it looked like it was gold.

So he didn't have nothing to do but teach the band. So he wanted to get involved with something else. So he went around to different classes to see who would want to get in and do a class of music, public school music. So when he came to my class, I raised my hand. Because see, I had had...

I forgot to tell this about my early years of school in Muskogee. We had a teacher. I don't know where she come from. Her name was Mrs. Clark. And she taught us... She taught us so many... I mean, we were just young kids. Man, she was teaching the theory of music. And the reason... That's the only reason I learned as much as I did about music. There was one girl especially. Her name was Lydia. I just didn't want... For some reason, I didn't want her to know no more about music than I did. And I didn't study
Thomas - 15
piano or nothing, but just the basic part of music. I don't know I was getting crazy about it, but I took it in public school.

So when Mr. Dawson came around trying to find somebody to get in public school music, I raised my hand and got in the class. So the first day, he gave a little speech. Now, he's a young teacher, too. He's just getting his feet wet teaching. So he asked, 'Anybody know how to write a scale?' I threw up my hand." He said, 'Well, go to the blackboard.' Now, to this day, I can't honestly say what scale he asked me to write. But to me, if I can remember, it was a scale he thought was hard, either E-flat or the key of E, something with three flats or four flats, or three sharps or four sharps. But it didn't make no difference...
And you had to construct it.

Yeah. But it didn't make no difference to me what scale either. Because we learned how to make scales, and the first thing we did was write them five lines, which gave you four spaces, and you'd write the G-clef, and then the next thing you'd do is write your signature. If it's three flats, you write your flats first. And then you start on the first line and write the key of E, E-flat. If it's A-flat, you start... You don't have to write no more signatures, because that thing at the beginning donates
Thomas - 16

[sic: denotes] what the note is. See, I knew that! So I don't know... I did it so fast, I often wonder...I have often wondered what did he actually think of me. So after class he told me to stay. I thought I had got in trouble. So he asked me to stay after school. So he said, "Would you like to get in the band?" See, he didn't have too many recruits for the band either. I said, "Yes." So he said, "Well, come to the band practice," whatever day it was, Tuesday or Thursday.
I got to the band practice. And I'll bet you can't guess what instrument...the first instrument he gave me to play.
The piccolo?

No. That was the second. He gave me a pair of cymbals. And he showed how to beat them. He said, "You hit them, and let them go away so they can ring." And the reason the cymbals were so easy, you just read along with the bass, and at the end sometimes they'd have a cymbal marking and you strike the cymbal. And that was about the easiest thing.

So after about three or four lessons, he... I think he... I really think he was testing me out to see if I was really interested in getting into music. So after about three or four band practices, he took me to the band room.
Thomas - 17

At first he asked me, "Would you like to play another horn?" I said, "Yes!" I'm in the band; I'm playin' my cymbals. So he looked over there, and he had a bugle horn. He said, "Would you like to play that?" Anything! Because I'm so glad he didn't pick up a clarinet, because them clarinets are so hard to play.

So he gave me the bugle horn. And I guess he must have gave me a book, you know, with the fingering. And after a few sessions with the bugle horn, and after I'd got a little embrochure... That was easy, because usually when you're reading the bugle horn, it really doesn't teach you how to read, because so many times you have a rest... He taught us how to... He's the first one that taught me how to count a rest out. He said, "You count... You've got four bars. You say, 'one-two-three-four,' 'two-two-three-four,' 'three-two-three-four,' 'four-two-three-four,' BOOM." And I just carried that over later on, because if you keep putting that next number after every bar, you'll know how far it is. But if you just start counting, you know...
[PAUSE: TELEPHONE]
So he taught you guys how to count.
Right. So I got to fool with this bugle horn. And he explained to me that the bugle horn was the third to... I had a feeling that I wanted to play something with
Thomas - 18

the piano. So he said with the bugle horn, you transpose a third down, a minor third down. And when he showed that to me, that was an easy transposition, because if a note is on the second line on the piano, your note will be on the first line for you. The only thing that you have to change is the signature. It don't (?). And it's funny about how that makes a note, even when you... If you've got an A-flat, your note will be F-natural. And if you've got an A-natural, your note will be F-sharp; you've got to make the tone(?) there. So that classification was easy. And do you know, I started transposing piano parts so I could play my bugle horn along with the piano? And when I think about it, that's when I first got involved with arranging.

And I had... See, I didn't have no idea I had this talent for music. But in Oklahoma, in them early days, we heard so many good bands nad good Blues players, and guys played piano. Alphonso Trent's band used to come through there, and he had a great band. And I heard this, and that music was kind of in my ear. But I didn't discern(?) it until I started to fool around with it.

So making a long story short, another pupil in the school had a saxophone. I wasn't satisfied just playing this bugle horn. I didn't have sense enough maybe to move up to a trumpet. So I asked him would he... Now, this was
Thomas - 19

my first at the school. So I asked him would he show me a scale on the saxophone. So he did. And when he showed me that, I thought that was quite easy. The C, middle-C is your middle finger, the second finger on the top, and then B-natural change over, and then the rest of the notes you put one finger down at a time -- A, G, F, E, D, C.

I wasn't satisfied, though. I did that for a few days, maybe a week or so. So I asked him... I had sense enough to ask him to show me the chromatic scale. Because I figured I'd got so far in music then, that I know if I got the chromatic scale, I'd have all the notes. And the octave... You'd just raise the octave key to get the notes up higher. He showed me the chromatic scale. And Milt, I don't know the exact time, but as near as I can remember, in three or four months, I was playing that saxophone good enough to play for a little school dance. Just from ear. I had this ear. I picked up whatever songs they was playing there... And by it being a C-melody, there was no transposition involved. So I just played along with the piano. Whatever was on the piano, I could play on the...on the tenor. And I needed time(?) to play my little Jazz... I often wish I could hear some of that Jazz I was playing then; it wasn't nothin'. So...
So you were set(?).
Thomas - 20

Yeah, but I was involved with... And I found out I had this talent. So when I went home the next summer on the break of school, I got my mother to buy me my first horn. I'll never forget it. The name of the music store was Jenkins. And they sent off... And it looked like it took forever. It only took about two or three weeks, because I think Jenkins' head store was in Kansas City. So in about two weeks I had my horn. And I had been telling all of my friends around Muskogee, "Man, I can play the saxophone," but none of them didn't believe me.

So when I got that horn, my own new horn, boy, I was gone. That next year, when I went back to school with my own horn, I had it made. Because I could practice all I wanted to and... About the second, maybe it was the third year in school, I started giggin'... Because we had a little band in school, too. We had a guy who played trumpet, and we got together. But by about the third year in school, I started playing with a band in Topeka. I guess saxophone players were hard to find in them days! So I started playing with the band in Topeka. I just played maybe one gig a week. I think the most i made was five dollars. And we didn't know about no unions then...
So I finished school, and I got good marks in carpentry. I had been into the carpentry trade... Because
Thomas - 21

the last year in school, like from your junior to your senior year in school, I stayed in school and worked. This was a school you could work and make money, too. They wouldn't give you actual money, but it would go on your tuition. Guess what our tuition was. For an out-of-state pupil, your tuition was eighteen dollars a month, and for in-state pupils I think it was fourteen dollars. And I always figured it was worth eighteen dollars for your parents to get rid of you, because you got your... That was for board and lodging.
Yeah!

Now, we were in ROTC, and they furnished us uniforms for ROTC, so it wasn't no big deal of buying any clothes. Because I remember when graduation came, my mother wanted to buy me a suit. I said, "You don't have to buy me no suit." Because we had a tailor shop there, and the tailor made the suits. Because see, that was practice. That was practice for the students that was taking tailoring. And that tailor was good. He was another guy from Tuskegee.

And you know, another beautiful thing about that school. They had houses for the teachers that had families. Because I know Mr. Burke had a pretty big family. He was originally a wheelwright, but he taught carpentry. And
Thomas - 22
he...
What's a wheelwright?
A wheelwright is a guy that makes wagons. And you know, he kept telling us about he's a wheelwright and... And I tell this about...
What did he tell you?
He told us about being a wheelwright. So he actually made a wagon. He made them wheels and spokes, and he made a wagon. He was a good carpentry teacher. He knew carpentry, too.

And another beautiful thing about taking carpentry, that last year we got a chance to actually build the houses. We'd build houses on the campus. And they had a pretty big little campus. For a prep school...you know what I mean, for...
What was the name of that school?
Kansas Vocational College.
Did we go out there once?
I think we did. I think we was in Tuskegee, and we went out there.
Yeah.
And oh, it was a pretty campus. We was kind of on a hill...
I remember that campus.
Thomas - 23
And another thing, a lady right off the campus had a little...a little store.
[END OF TAPE 1, SIDE A]

It wasn't a restaurant. But the best thing she made was chili. So if we ever missed... If we missed dinner at school, as long as we had a quarter in our pockets, we could go down to... I can't think of her name. We could down there. And boy, she made the best chili. See, Topeka had a lot of Mexicans in it, because that's where the home town for the Topeka...Santa Fe...
The railroad?

The Topeka and Santa Fe. That was the home town, and that's where they built that road. So they brought in a lot of Mexicans. And where there was Mexicans, you had hot tamales and chili. Because we had a guy down in Topeka named Robey; he had the best chili. But this woman, she made chili just as good as the Mexicans did it. We'd get crackers, put them in there, and the stuff would be in you...
Foots, I want to ask you about... Before we get all the way out of school, just go back a little bit about your family, about your mother and your father. What
Thomas - 24
did your father do for a living?
Well, my father was a... Oh, he was an all-around man. He cut... He took care of lawns. He cooked in...
In restaurants?

No, he was at home. And my mother was the most sensational cook.. I often... I asked my sister. My mother...I couldn't understand it. She never had too much formal training. But she could cook. She made the best pies and cakes...
How many were you all?
Well, there was four of us. I have two brothers and one sister.
What's your sister's name?
Cleora. And my brother is George. You've met George.
Yeah, I've met George.
And Joe. And we had a couple of more in my family that passed on. Because there was a daughter that was next to me; she passed.
Well, how did your father support ...(?)...
Well, my father worked for some family in Muskogee. This guy, I think, was a candy salesman or something. And we had a home free. Evidently he owned that
Thomas - 25

property we was on. We didn't pay no rent. And we learned to get out and cut grass, and my mother used to do laundry and do that baking stuff. Because in my senior year, between my junior and senior year...
Because they had the money to buy a saxophone.

Right. Yeah, because my mother was doing work, and I used to... I delivered many a bundle of laundry. We had a horse... Man, when I think of it, we was loaded! We had a horse, we had chickens, hogs... And my grandfather used to come in every Fall and help kill the hogs. And he had a smokehouse... Milt, you haven't tasted no meat yet until you taste how he smoked that meat. And he knew how to make syrup out of cane... My grandfather was... He grew the best okra. He was a farmer at heart, but he was just a vagabond! He just liked to travel from one place to another. And he was more fond, I guess, of his younger daughter, because he stayed with her more than anybody, and he was crazy about my mother because she was the oldest of them.
And that's how we got along. Because actually, my mother had them big pots where she would wash the clothes, put the clothes in there and soak it and all that...
In the back yard.
Thomas - 26
Right. And we would deliver it, because we had a horse-and-wagon. So we delivered it...
[INAUDIBLE]

I learned how to ride when I was a young kid. I learned how to ride bareback, almost like the Indians. And I had a horse. I could ride him out three or four miles. And boy, when that sucker he was going home, he'd take off. I'd just let him alone and just let him go, and hold on to stay on, you know. When he got back home, he slowed up. But he knew the way back home, too. I didn't have to guide him or nothin'!

And we had a... We lived a block away from the pavement. We had streetcars... Oklahoma really built up fast. I don't really know... I guess it's on account of finding oil down there. See, because when they found the oil, everybody started coming in. That's how they got all them good teachers. We had a beautiful high school and a beautiful grade school, and we had schools in all the different parts of the town. We were close to one of those forts that...
Which fort was that?
Fort Gibson. And we got to know all the Indians, because it was the beginning of the Oklahoma... At first, Oklahoma was called the Indian Territory, and then

segments.title: Opening: Milt Hinton begins the interview for the Smithsonian
segments.summary: Hinton states the date and introduces his friend Walter P. Thomas; they joke about the middle initial and Foots's nickname.

segments.title: Born in Muskogee, Oklahoma, 1907; parents and siblings
segments.summary: Thomas gives his birth date, the Oklahoma statehood land giveaway, his siblings George and Cleora born in Texas, and his parents' names and origins.

segments.title: Grandfather's Oklahoma homesteading story and its lesson
segments.summary: His grandfather, a former slave, sold his Texas land to homestead in Oklahoma but was too religious to claim it; Thomas says this taught him to get an education.

segments.title: Kindergarten, failing math, and the sixth-grade teacher who turned him around
segments.summary: He remembers kindergarten music, failing fifth-grade math, being promoted on condition, excelling under a teacher he later thanked, and the value of fractions.

segments.title: Going away to high school in Topeka and falling for math
segments.summary: He persuades his mother to send him to a school in Topeka, where good teachers make algebra and geometry click and he takes four years of math.

segments.title: Mr. Drury, Latin and the valedictorian speech
segments.summary: Teacher Mr. Drury unexpectedly teaches Latin, steadies the class, and patiently helps Thomas write his valedictorian speech.

segments.title: Mr. Drury's lessons in economics and banking
segments.summary: Drury taught economics and public speaking; Thomas recalls laws of supply and demand, runs on banks, and how to establish credit, and complains about modern economic leaders.

segments.title: Drury's drama class and why teachers matter
segments.summary: Drury insisted the students could enter any college and coached Thomas as Dr. Rank in A Doll's House; Thomas calls teachers the greatest influence on a life.

segments.title: Carpentry, Kansas Vocational Institute and band teacher William L. Dawson
segments.summary: Intending architecture, Thomas studies carpentry at the Tuskegee-style Kansas Vocational Institute, whose first band teacher, William L. Dawson, has a beautiful trombone tone.

segments.title: Dawson's music class: writing a scale at the board and playing cymbals
segments.summary: Earlier theory lessons in Muskogee let Thomas write a scale at the blackboard; Dawson invites him into the band and starts him on cymbals.

segments.title: The bugle horn, counting rests and first transposing
segments.summary: Dawson moves him to the bugle horn, teaches him to count rests, and transposing piano parts for it is his first arranging.

segments.title: Teaching himself saxophone and gigging in Topeka
segments.summary: Hearing Alphonso Trent's band in Oklahoma, he learns C-melody sax from a schoolmate, buys his first horn from Jenkins, and by the third year plays a weekly gig in Topeka.

segments.title: School life at Kansas Vocational: tuition, ROTC, building houses
segments.summary: He describes working for tuition, ROTC uniforms, the tailor shop, carpentry teacher Mr. Burke the wheelwright, building campus houses, and a neighbor's chili.

segments.title: His parents' work and the Thomas family
segments.summary: Thomas describes his father as an all-around man, his mother's cooking, his siblings Cleora, George and Joe, and the free house they lived in.

segments.title: Farm life, laundry deliveries and growing up in Muskogee
segments.summary: His mother's laundry business funded his saxophone; he recalls the horse and wagon, hog killing with his grandfather, riding bareback, and Oklahoma's oil-driven growth.

segments.title: Brothers George and Joe; band hometown hospitality
segments.summary: Questions on his brother George's age and birthplace lead to Joe's youthful mischief and the band tradition of being entertained in each musician's home town.

segments.title: Oklahoma oil-rich Indians and an oilman who pitched Cab Calloway
segments.summary: Thomas tells of a woman whose land produced a million barrels a day and a part-Indian oilman who tried to sell Cab stock in Longview, Texas.

segments.title: Sister at Oberlin and his mother as a hotel baker
segments.summary: His sister attended Oberlin, which made him want to go; his mother baked at a Muskogee hotel and he ate hot rolls there.

segments.title: Fresh chicken, cream on bread, and working his way through school
segments.summary: He recalls eating farm-fresh food, unable later to eat store-bought chicken in New York, and cleaning the academic building to pay tuition.

segments.title: Hired by Kid Carter's band in Minot, North Dakota
segments.summary: Overstreet in Topeka gets him a telegram offer; he travels to Minot to join Kid Carter's four-piece band playing one-night dances, including reels and square dances.

segments.title: His father's advice, wool underwear and Art Graham
segments.summary: His father gives advice and long underwear for North Dakota; Thomas reads piano parts on C-melody, and Art Graham from St. Paul joins and outplays him.

segments.title: Touring the Dakotas, Black Hills and West with Kid Carter
segments.summary: Riding by car on short jumps through the Black Hills, Bismarck, Colorado and Utah, he sees Custer's monument, the Grand Canyon and Indian girls.

segments.title: Studying hard, dorm life and giving up piano
segments.summary: He reflects that missing out on land made him study; describes dormitory routine and how a girlfriend caused him to miss piano lessons.

segments.title: Moose Jaw, Saskatchewan: college plans lost to a good paying job
segments.summary: Playing a cafe in Moose Jaw, he is befriended by white kids, plays basketball at the YMCA, registers for college, but takes the band money instead and never goes.

segments.title: Minneapolis with Clarence Johnson and meeting Bill Pugh
segments.summary: Thomas moves to the Twin Cities to play with pianist Clarence Johnson, who could not read; he recalls a trumpeter hired by Trent just for blues and Hinton's tie to Bill Pugh.

segments.title: Learning to read from a theater saxophonist in Minneapolis
segments.summary: A pit-band saxophonist gets him through a big study book; his bugle-horn transposition carries over to alto, and Thomas credits mathematics and Schillinger.

segments.title: Meeting Lester Young and his family in Minneapolis
segments.summary: Thomas recalls dance work around the Twin Cities and meeting Prez, his father and brother Lee, then seeing Lester with King Oliver in Kansas City and finding him scared of New York.

segments.title: Idols Frankie Trumbauer and Red Nichols
segments.summary: The two recall Trumbauer's C-melody solo on 'Singin' the Blues' and Thomas's admiration for Red Nichols and his Five Pennies.

segments.title: Minneapolis as a regional meeting place; the Pettiford family
segments.summary: They discuss Minneapolis as the music hub near Omaha and Des Moines and Thomas recalls meeting the Pettiford family, including Oscar and Killer, in Oklahoma.

segments.title: What Minneapolis gave him: reading, math and gratitude to teachers
segments.summary: Thomas and Hinton agree that reading and math underlay their careers, and Thomas thanks teachers like Drury; they mention Will Vodery.

segments.chapter: Chicago, Ohio and Jelly Roll Morton
segments.title: Chicago, Wallace Bishop's house and first recording with Jelly Roll Morton
segments.summary: He lands at drummer Wallace Bishop's house in Chicago, where Jelly Roll Morton finds him and records with Bishop's group around 1926-27.

segments.chapter: Chicago, Ohio and Jelly Roll Morton
segments.title: Ohio: the job in Ada, meeting his wife in Lima and the Mills Brothers
segments.summary: After Cleveland he plays a frat-house job in Ada, Ohio, meets his future wife in Lima, joins his first union and meets the Mills Brothers.

segments.chapter: Chicago, Ohio and Jelly Roll Morton
segments.title: Jelly inspires him to write; college dates in Pennsylvania
segments.summary: Watching Jelly write music pushes him to try arranging, and a Pennsylvania booker gets Jelly's band into ballrooms and colleges.

segments.chapter: Chicago, Ohio and Jelly Roll Morton
segments.title: Jelly sends for him in New York: the saxophone section
segments.summary: Called from Indiana to be third alto in Jelly's New York band beside Russell Procope, Joe Garland and Al Sears.

segments.chapter: Chicago, Ohio and Jelly Roll Morton
segments.title: Arriving in New York, 1928, and the Virginia clique in Jelly's band
segments.summary: Thomas recalls arriving through the tunnel, his first subway ride, Jelly meeting him in Harlem, and the band wondering who the new little alto was.

segments.chapter: Chicago, Ohio and Jelly Roll Morton
segments.title: Playing Jelly's stop-chorus dance arrangements; Tommy Benford
segments.summary: He describes the chorus-by-chorus modulating dance format, Jelly's out-of-state status, and Tommy Benford on drums.

segments.chapter: Chicago, Ohio and Jelly Roll Morton
segments.title: Jelly Roll's character and taking the road with him
segments.summary: Thomas finds Jelly braggadocious but truthful, quotes his rule 'If you get lost, lay out,' and says he alone of the New York men went on the road.

segments.chapter: Chicago, Ohio and Jelly Roll Morton
segments.title: Arthur Melrose and Jelly's recording and publishing deal
segments.summary: Melrose, a white publisher, arranged Jelly's Victor recording and took the copyrights; Jelly cared only about getting popular and could call for cash.

segments.chapter: Chicago, Ohio and Jelly Roll Morton
segments.title: Recording at Victor's Camden studio; band members and Frazier's quip
segments.summary: The band records in Camden under the Victor dog, with Jelly writing parts; Thomas recalls trumpeter Richardson and bassist Frazier.

segments.chapter: Chicago, Ohio and Jelly Roll Morton
segments.title: Driving Jelly's brakeless bus into New York
segments.summary: As the band breaks up, Thomas drives the bus into Manhattan, stopped by a cop in Central Park and stopping it against curbs.

segments.chapter: Chicago, Ohio and Jelly Roll Morton
segments.title: Freddy Jenkins, joining Local 802 and the Joe Steele job
segments.summary: Friend Freddy Jenkins cannot lend the fifty-dollar union fee, so Thomas plays two weeks at pianist Joe Steele's Seventh Avenue club while the union man is away and then pays to join Local 802.

segments.title: How he got into the Missourians when Scotty went to jail
segments.summary: Saxophonist Scotty gets six months under the Sullivan Law for carrying a gun, and the Missourians, prompted by Kansas City trumpeter Lamar Wright, call Thomas as a temporary replacement.

segments.title: Writing down the Missourians' head arrangements; Cozy Cole's dance-school band
segments.summary: Finding the band plays only head arrangements, Thomas starts writing parts and sells his first arrangements to Cozy Cole; he also recalls Omar Simeon from Jelly's band.

segments.title: Jelly Roll's explanation: melody from New Orleans, beat from Latin America
segments.summary: Thomas relays Jelly's view that jazz melody came from New Orleans and the beat from the Latin countries; Hinton argues the beat came from Africa.

segments.title: Why New Orleans players sounded alike: Noone, Ory and a piano-trumpet man
segments.summary: Thomas discusses early New Orleans arpeggio-based playing, a Minneapolis trumpeter who copied Louis, clarinetists like Simeon and Noone, and Noone's praise of Kid Ory.

segments.title: The Missourians' personnel and sound
segments.summary: He describes the Missourians as three brass, three saxes and rhythm with tuba player Smitty and trumpet soloist R.Q. Dickerson; Benny Carter arrangements were brought in.

segments.title: A cooperative band that cut the Savoy's bands; Lockwood as front man
segments.summary: The Missourians had worked the Cotton Club, hired leaders such as Lockwood, beat all comers at the Savoy and Alhambra, and earned fifty dollars a week.

segments.title: Cab Calloway comes in from the Alabamians and Blackbirds; Irving Mills
segments.summary: After the Alabamians failed and Cab left a show, the Missourians pay him to front them; Irving Mills takes an interest and Thomas grows close to Cab.

segments.title: Lessons with Merle Johnson and the Cotton Club break replacing Duke
segments.summary: Following Cab's lead, Thomas studies saxophone with Merle Johnson; the band gets the Cotton Club job when Duke Ellington goes to film Three Little Words.

segments.title: Covering for Andrew Brown and moving to tenor
segments.summary: When Andrew Brown falls sick Thomas takes his solos on tenor, and the band diplomatically reassigns Brown to alto and Thomas to tenor.

segments.title: Cab's 'Play it, Foots!' and earlier work with Luis Russell
segments.summary: Cab's shouts made Thomas famous; he recalls playing earlier with Luis Russell's New Orleans players, which fed his ad-lib style.

segments.title: Studying with Andrew Jacobson in Boston
segments.summary: Milt remembers waiting while Thomas took lessons with Jacobson, who taught relaxing the tongue on attack; Thomas explains how he found him through Henry Williams.

segments.title: Subtones, the Selmer saxophone and Merle's advice
segments.summary: Thomas explains Jacobson's subtones, keeping one embouchure across registers, why Selmers carry, and Merle's saying that sound comes from the way you blow.

segments.title: Jacobson's perfect attack and Thomas's teaching ambitions
segments.summary: He calls Jacobson a genius, describes the tongue-on-reed attack, and says he wanted to teach only after studying with him; a Kansas professor is mentioned.

segments.title: Teaching the Cab saxophone section; playing solos for absent soloists
segments.summary: Brown and Hilton Jefferson study with Merle; Thomas takes a back seat to Chu Berry and Ben Webster and can still cover for absent soloists such as Illinois Jacquet.

segments.title: Cab takes over the band; who was in the Missourians
segments.summary: In Philadelphia Cab tells the band he will take it over or hire another, so billing changes to Cab Calloway and His Orchestra; Thomas lists the Missourians' members.

segments.title: Morris White's perfect tempo and his marriage to W.C. Handy's daughter
segments.summary: The band tests guitarist Morris White's time against a metronome and he passes; he married Handy's youngest daughter Lil.

segments.title: 'Hi-De-Ho', 'Willie the Weeper' and how Foots wrote the 'Minnie the Moocher' arrangement
segments.summary: Mills adapted the public-domain 'Willie the Weeper' as 'Minnie the Moocher'; Cab asked Thomas to fix a failed arrangement and he wrote the intro overnight, echoing 'Get Happy'.

segments.title: Repetition and sequence in composing; realizing his own talent
segments.summary: Thomas credits his teacher Timothy with the idea that listeners need repetition and sequence, and reflects that music talent surfaced only after he began playing.

segments.chapter: Cotton Club and radio fame with Cab
segments.title: The Cotton Club: gangsters, Walter Winchell and George Raft
segments.summary: He recalls tiring of 'Minnie the Moocher' for Winchell, Owney Madden's ownership with Herman Stark as front man, and George Raft dancing to 'Sweet Georgia Brown'.

segments.chapter: Cotton Club and radio fame with Cab
segments.title: Radio airtime from the Duke Ellington break
segments.summary: The Cotton Club broadcasts on CBS and NBC made the band; Thomas wanders into network ownership before Hinton steers back to music.

segments.chapter: Cotton Club and radio fame with Cab
segments.title: Receiving notice from Moe Gale
segments.summary: While Duke is away, the band is reorganized and Moe Gale gives Thomas two weeks' notice, which Mills overturns.

segments.chapter: Cotton Club and radio fame with Cab
segments.title: Big Broadcast of 1934 and Bing Crosby at the Paramount
segments.summary: Mills gets the band the Bing Crosby film; Thomas recalls playing the Paramount with Bing as extra attraction and Cab's friction with Bing's brother.

segments.chapter: Cotton Club and radio fame with Cab
segments.title: The gangsters wreck a rival Harlem club
segments.summary: A would-be rival club on 125th Street that ignored the Cotton Club's warning is vandalized overnight, so the show never opens.

segments.chapter: Cotton Club and radio fame with Cab
segments.title: Alternating with Duke, the Duffy payoff and 'Minnie' becomes the theme
segments.summary: Cab and Duke trade the Cotton Club between road tours, the downtown club is arranged by giving Duffy 25 percent, and the band discovers its theme song on the road.

segments.chapter: Cotton Club and radio fame with Cab
segments.title: Harold Arlen, 'Stormy Weather', Ethel Waters and Lena Horne
segments.summary: Thomas and Hinton recall Arlen writing Cotton Club shows, Ethel Waters introducing 'Stormy Weather', and Lena Horne copying her.

segments.chapter: Cotton Club and radio fame with Cab
segments.title: How bands made singers: Sinatra and Bing Crosby
segments.summary: Thomas says bands made more singers than anyone; he credits Tommy Dorsey for Sinatra's phrasing and idolizes Bing Crosby, whose records he bought.

segments.chapter: Cotton Club and radio fame with Cab
segments.title: Recording 'Minnie the Moocher' with Victor Young
segments.summary: The Cotton Club moves downtown; Thomas recalls the session where his strip-paper arrangement was slowed down on Victor Young's suggestion that a minor sounds better slow.

segments.chapter: Cotton Club and radio fame with Cab
segments.title: Harold Arlen's Black blues feeling
segments.summary: Thomas says Arlen had the blues talent; they discuss 'Stormy Weather', 'Get Happy', Arlen as a rehearsal pianist and singer, and his Cotton Club shows.

segments.title: How Milt Hinton came into Cab's band in Chicago
segments.summary: Hinton recalls Cab hearing him at the Three Deuces on Keg Johnson's recommendation after bassist Al Morgan stayed in California.

segments.title: Looking after the new bassist on the road
segments.summary: Thomas remembers Lamar Wright sending ahead for rooms and persuading a landlady in the Midwest to take in Hinton.

segments.title: Saving Hinton's job when the union tore up his Chicago card
segments.summary: The Local 802 man rejects Hinton's card at the Cotton Club rehearsal; Thomas, knowing the rules, keeps him working two days a week until his six months were up.

segments.title: The Eddie Barefield union letter and the Cotton Club's $80 deal
segments.summary: Thomas gets Barefield into Local 802 with a letter from a defunct union and explains the Cotton Club's deal with the union to pay eighty dollars a week.

segments.title: Hustling as assistant director: plugging songs for publishers
segments.summary: Unpaid as assistant director, Thomas screens songwriters' material, gets ten dollars per radio play, and learns how plugging builds hits.

segments.title: Airchecks, balance and song pluggers
segments.summary: Thomas introduced airchecks to Cab, learned microphone balance from them, and remembers pluggers such as Bubbles Durgham.

segments.title: Conducting with a saxophone and learning to conduct
segments.summary: The Cotton Club show writers decide to write Thomas out of the band and make him conductor; he studies conducting and gets a tuxedo.

segments.title: Healy, Helen Morgan, Wallace Beery and the improved shows
segments.summary: Thomas recalls producer Healy's celebrity Sundays, a drunk Helen Morgan, Wallace Beery's ovation, and getting Harold Arlen to write full show music.

segments.title: Personnel of the first downtown Cotton Club band, 1936
segments.summary: Hinton and Thomas reconstruct the rhythm section, saxophones, trombones and trumpets of the 1936 band.

segments.title: Will Vodery's lessons on scoring and accompanying singers
segments.summary: A veteran arranger told the band to stay under the singer and to score in ink, checking every four bars; he reportedly had Gershwin as copyist.

segments.title: Bawling out Cab during the Bill Robinson show
segments.summary: While conducting the Cotton Club show, Thomas rebukes a nervous Cab for heckling, later apologizes, and explains Cab picked up bawling out from Rudy Vallee.

segments.title: Leaving Cab: Greely Walton replaces him and he joins Don Redman
segments.summary: Having a job lined up, Thomas gives notice, Cab insists he find a replacement, and he finds Greely Walton before going with Redman.

segments.chapter: Arrangers, Bill Robinson and Coleman Hawkins
segments.title: Cotton Club show order; pushing Benny Carter arrangements; Doc Cheatham
segments.summary: They list the alternating Cab and Duke shows and Thomas tries to get Cab to buy Benny Carter arrangements, praising Doc Cheatham.

segments.chapter: Arrangers, Bill Robinson and Coleman Hawkins
segments.title: Conducting two Cotton Club shows
segments.summary: Thomas says he conducted two shows after writers made it look like a Broadway production, and rehearsed his short announcing speech.

segments.chapter: Arrangers, Bill Robinson and Coleman Hawkins
segments.title: Bill Robinson, Ben Webster and ballads
segments.summary: Thomas recalls playing Robinson's tune on flute, Bojangles dancing equally on both feet, Ben Webster's laughter, and Ben as a great ballad player.

segments.chapter: Arrangers, Bill Robinson and Coleman Hawkins
segments.title: Interludes from Jelly Roll and writing for his own record dates
segments.summary: Thomas credits Jelly for his use of interludes, tailors progressions to Jonah Jones and Charlie Shavers, and recalls the first solo he took on a record.

segments.chapter: Arrangers, Bill Robinson and Coleman Hawkins
segments.title: Staying in Coleman Hawkins' mother's house in St. Joe
segments.summary: As a school basketball player Thomas stayed in Hawkins' family house in St. Joseph and learned Hawkins started on cello.

segments.chapter: Arrangers, Bill Robinson and Coleman Hawkins
segments.title: Coleman Hawkins' styles and Benny Carter's influence
segments.summary: Thomas argues Benny Carter influenced Hawkins' melodic turn and describes Hawkins as the man who made tenor saxophone respectable.

segments.chapter: Arrangers, Bill Robinson and Coleman Hawkins
segments.title: Hawkins' return from Europe and 'Body and Soul'
segments.summary: Thomas describes musicians dismissing Hawkins after Europe and his answer with 'Body and Soul', a solo modulating through three keys.

segments.chapter: Arrangers, Bill Robinson and Coleman Hawkins
segments.title: Recording four tunes for Joe Davis with Coleman Hawkins
segments.summary: Thomas hires Hawkins for a hundred dollars a day, writes progressions for four tunes, and finds he reads the piano part.

segments.chapter: Arrangers, Bill Robinson and Coleman Hawkins
segments.title: Hawkins at a 52nd Street club; his friendship; Benny Carter's talent
segments.summary: Thomas asks Hawkins to play 'Body and Soul' on 52nd Street, notes the money-minded Hawkins, and praises Benny Carter's natural writing.

segments.chapter: After Cab: Don Redman, teaching and records
segments.title: Why he left Cab: wanting to teach; Don Redman
segments.summary: With a baby coming, Thomas leaves the road, remembering Don Redman as a giant writer who loved quarts of ice cream.

segments.chapter: After Cab: Don Redman, teaching and records
segments.title: Art Tatum in Toledo and at the Cotton Club
segments.summary: Thomas recalls hearing Tatum in a Toledo alley restaurant, getting him to play the Cotton Club, and Tatum's card tricks.

segments.chapter: After Cab: Don Redman, teaching and records
segments.title: His small band at the Zanzibar and first record
segments.summary: After Redman, Thomas fronts a small band at the Zanzibar, records 'Poor But Happy', loses his piano player Clyde Hart one night, and resents being billed under another name.

segments.chapter: After Cab: Don Redman, teaching and records
segments.title: Teaching studio with Cozy Cole and his pupils
segments.summary: Thomas and Cozy Cole open a 48th Street studio, he advertises as ex-Cab, and teaches Wyler and Buddy Stafford.

segments.chapter: After Cab: Don Redman, teaching and records
segments.title: Ending the studio; publishing; BMI deal; losing his Joe Davis rights
segments.summary: The studio lasts two years, a publishing firm folds, and Thomas explains how he lost royalties on his Joe Davis records.

segments.chapter: After Cab: Don Redman, teaching and records
segments.title: How reissues of his records cost him royalties
segments.summary: He recounts handing over scores, a lost letter promising royalties from Prestige, a collector's cleaned-up tape, and being swindled, like Jelly.

segments.chapter: After Cab: Don Redman, teaching and records
segments.title: Moe Gale's 'holding company' and late recording payments
segments.summary: The band was paid a year after recording, with Gale keeping the interest.

segments.chapter: After Cab: Don Redman, teaching and records
segments.title: Paying the band in odd change and the savings-account idea
segments.summary: As paymaster at $66.66 a week, Thomas drew exact change and proposed a band savings account, which the men soon quit.

segments.chapter: After Cab: Don Redman, teaching and records
segments.title: Doubling money: theatre dates and the Big Broadcast earnings
segments.summary: He imagines what a band bank would have grown to, describes doubling pay and the hourly film scale, and a California tour cancelled.

segments.chapter: After Cab: Don Redman, teaching and records
segments.title: The lost Stormy Weather record with Benny Carter and Jacquet
segments.summary: He recalls a California recording with Benny Carter, Illinois Jacquet and Hilton Jefferson that none of them has, and noisy old records.

segments.title: Starting personal management with Dizzy Gillespie
segments.summary: Teaching led to managing; Dizzy gave him a year, and Thomas advised Dizzy to go to England first as a single.

segments.title: Snooky's, Morris Levy and Dizzy's house loan
segments.summary: Thomas books Dizzy at Snooky's when Levy won't pay more, then gets Levy to lend six thousand dollars and raise him to fifteen hundred.

segments.title: How Dizzy Gillespie's bent horn happened
segments.summary: The horn fell off the piano at Snooky's and was bent; the repairman said it would break, so Dizzy kept it.

segments.title: Booking Bill Davis and Billy Shaw's commission
segments.summary: Thomas begins booking organist Bill Davis, and works with Billy Shaw on a five percent commission.

segments.title: Touring with Bill Davis and running his own booking office
segments.summary: He manages Bill Davis in California for a hundred dollars and expenses and back home runs his own saxophone-studio booking office.

segments.title: Joining Billy Shaw's agency; Bill Davis at Birdland; Joe Glaser
segments.summary: Shaw persuades him to become an agent; he gets Bill Davis into Birdland and recalls Joe Glaser wanting big records.

segments.title: Making 'April in Paris' with Bill Davis and Bill Jennings
segments.summary: Thomas suggests the tune, fixes bass recording, and the 'one more time' ending later made famous by Basie.

segments.title: Booking for Shaw: what Calloway taught him
segments.summary: He explains why booking appealed, how Cab's work taught him to book, and that Bill Davis wouldn't listen when getting twenty-five hundred dollars.

segments.title: Bill Jennings, left-handed guitarist
segments.summary: Thomas describes Jennings learning guitar upside down from his right-handed brother, rumors of his troubles, and urging him to play softer.

segments.title: Acoustics: play softly, bass overtones and noise is not music
segments.summary: A California A&R man taught him to record softly; Thomas explains overtones and criticizes loud rock and disco.

segments.title: Booking Ray Charles on his first concert
segments.summary: Seeing Ray Charles play dances to poorly dressed crowds, Thomas books him on concerts and proposes a double of Newark and Carnegie Hall.

segments.title: Carnegie Hall double, Dinah Washington and Ray Charles as concert artist
segments.summary: Ray Charles accepts a thousand dollars for both dates, Thomas adds Dinah Washington, and Thursday at Connors Beach proves his concert appeal.

segments.title: Ray Charles the jazz artist; a flop Philadelphia date
segments.summary: Thomas learns Ray Charles had played with Lowell Fulsom and was really a jazz artist, and misbooks New York musicians for his first Philadelphia date.

segments.title: R&B audiences wanted singing, not jazz
segments.summary: At a Wilmington dance the crowd waited outside for Ray Charles, so Thomas tells him his band must play R&B.

segments.title: Booking territories and Thomas's best region
segments.summary: He explains how agencies divided territories and why his Richmond to Buffalo territory was the best in the country.

segments.title: Billy Shaw on commissions and the union rules
segments.summary: Shaw's fifteen percent arrangement, union limits on commissions, and the former 350-mile booking rule.

segments.title: Taking on Fats Domino and booking two weeks of dates
segments.summary: Given Domino in January, Thomas books him for two-week runs of Mondays through Thursdays in short jumps.

segments.title: Driving to Boston to hear Domino
segments.summary: Puzzled by how easy he was to book, Thomas drives to Boston, finds a New Orleans band and screaming fans, and predicts Domino will be as big as Fats Waller.

segments.title: White audiences and 'My Blue Heaven'
segments.summary: He finds white college kids know Domino's records and suggests recording a standard, which becomes 'My Blue Heaven'.

segments.title: Persuading Domino to play Las Vegas
segments.summary: Domino balked at six thousand dollars, but Thomas told him Vegas would set him for life; his gambling debt is mentioned.

segments.title: Rivalry with Dick Boom over booking
segments.summary: A competing agent resented Thomas for tying up territory, refused to book with him, then joined his office.

segments.title: B.B. King, Queen Booking and Ruth Bowen
segments.summary: Thomas regrets missing B.B. King and describes Ruth Bowen, his saxophone-studio tenant, becoming Dinah Washington's manager.

segments.title: Ruth Bowen's license, gangsters and missing contracts
segments.summary: Thomas explains how Joe Glaser helped Bowen get licensed, and her mistakes with gangsters and no contracts.

segments.title: Why Black agencies failed: Ray Charles, Joe Adams and John Lee
segments.summary: Thomas says Ray Charles now books himself, explains how his agency's new owner botched a complaint, and mentions John Lee managing Nancy Wilson.

segments.title: Advice on starting in personal management; why he has no license
segments.summary: Thomas advises getting the right agent, explains why he never took an agency license, and Bill Doggett and Bill Davis leaving him.

segments.title: Should a musician leave music for management?
segments.summary: Pressed by Hinton, Thomas says in hindsight he would have kept writing.

segments.title: Lessons from Calloway; Dizzy, Joe Carroll and Moody
segments.summary: He says Cab's band taught him booking and publicity, regrets losing Dizzy, and mentions Joe Carroll and James Moody.

segments.title: His hope to teach again and what he now knows about music
segments.summary: Without a degree, he plans to approach colleges and says he could have been a great arranger had he known earlier.

segments.title: Advice one: study mathematics
segments.summary: Thomas tells young musicians math is a perfect science that teaches thinking and that music is basically math.

segments.title: How failing fifth-grade math made him love it
segments.summary: He retells the conditional promotion, mastering fractions, and algebra and geometry as arithmetic that gave him a year of college math.

segments.title: Discovering Christian Science in Philadelphia
segments.summary: Seeking a church, he is advised to see a practitioner, who explains the Comforter promised in John.

segments.title: The age of the whole truth; healed of a cold
segments.summary: The practitioner calls this the age of Christian Science; Thomas studies it and is healed of a cold overnight.

segments.title: Timothy, a Christian Scientist teacher, on what music is
segments.summary: Hinton recalls reading Thomas's books; Thomas says Timothy taught that music is melody, harmony and rhythm and that discord is not music.

segments.title: Timothy's method: counterpoint and the three progressions
segments.summary: Thomas credits Timothy, a Schillinger pupil, for teaching counterpoint in six weeks and a mathematical view of progressions and the cycle of fifths.

segments.title: Lionel Hampton as a Christian Scientist
segments.summary: Thomas says Hampton is a Christian Scientist reportedly healed of drinking, who showed him how to do the lessons.

segments.title: Solomon's wisdom and learning the Bible
segments.summary: Thomas quotes Solomon on getting wisdom and understanding and says Christian Science made him study the whole Bible.

segments.title: Jimmy Blanton's tuberculosis in California
segments.summary: Hinton tells how Ben Webster asked him to look after Blanton, left sick in a California rest home when Duke's band moved on.

segments.title: Visiting Blanton and wishing they had known Christian Science
segments.summary: Hinton visited Blanton regularly with Chu Berry and Cozy Cole; Thomas regrets he was too new in Science to help properly.

segments.title: 'Man's extremity is God's opportunity'; Hinton's grandmother's hymns
segments.summary: They talk about faith, Hinton's churchgoing grandmother who was a slave, and her singing 'Amazing Grace'.

segments.title: Applying a spiritual principle to music: a chord written 96 ways
segments.summary: Thomas says putting into practice what you know led him to write one four-note chord 96 ways, and he believes jazz can be taught.

segments.title: Timothy: without repetition or sequence the listener is lost
segments.summary: He repeats Timothy's lesson and compares music to a rambling speaker.

segments.title: Advice: find your talent
segments.summary: Thomas urges finding where one's talent lies, citing student Oscar Cohen who went to Joe Glaser's mailroom, and his son the artist.

segments.title: Learning to pray; recap of his advice; the golf-lesson point on teachers
segments.summary: Thomas says Christian Science taught him to pray; Hinton sums up math, religion and talent; Thomas says a good teacher matters.

segments.title: Mary Baker Eddy: angels, discord is not music, and 'lay out'
segments.summary: Thomas links Eddy's line that discord is not music to Jelly's 'If you get lost, lay out' and they close on mental discipline.

segments.title: Joining the Missourians: Scotty's gun arrest and the corporation band
segments.summary: Opening Part 3, Thomas retells how Scotty's jail term opened a spot, how the corporation band worked, and how Lamar Wright knew him from Topeka.

segments.title: Cotton Club break when Duke went to California; the Savoy deal
segments.summary: The band took Duke's place, and the Savoy and Moe Gale's concessions paid fifty dollars a week.

segments.title: Lockwood Lewis and Cab Calloway's arrival
segments.summary: After front man Lockwood Lewis left, the band hired Cab, who came from the Alabamians and Blackbirds.

segments.title: Irving Mills, Moe Gale and the 'Minnie the Moocher' arrangement
segments.summary: Mills brought songs for his publishing house and had Mitchell Parrish write lyrics to 'Willie the Weeper'; the first arrangement fell flat.

segments.title: Writing the 'Minnie the Moocher' introduction overnight
segments.summary: Cab asked for an arrangement; Thomas wrote an eight-bar intro and ending on strips of paper.

segments.title: The recording session: the A&R man with perfect ears
segments.summary: Four tunes made a date; a brilliant A&R man stopped squeaks and suggested slowing the minor tune.

segments.title: Hilton Jefferson and the 'hi-de-ho' answers
segments.summary: Thomas laid out under Cab's singing and recalls coaxing stage-frightened Jeff to sing.

segments.title: Winchell, the theme song and the 1933 Europe trip
segments.summary: Asked for the year, Thomas says 1929-31 and Walter Winchell kept requesting the tune.

segments.title: Switching to tenor when Andrew Brown was ill
segments.summary: The sick Brown's solos pass to Thomas on tenor; when Brown returns he's given alto.

segments.title: How he got the nickname Foots
segments.summary: Thomas says small shoes caused foot trouble, and Cab's 'Play it, Foots!' stuck; he bought a tenor.

segments.title: Alternating with Duke uptown; 'Minnie' becomes a hit
segments.summary: The Cotton Club at 143rd Street and Lenox traded bands between Cab and Duke, and 'Minnie' became a hit on the road.

segments.title: Identifying the players in a 1930 band photograph
segments.summary: Hinton and Thomas identify the Missourians in a Rapido studio photo: Prince, Brown, Cab, Blue, White, Maxey, Dickerson, Wright, Smitty and Wheeler.

segments.title: What the band earned compared with ordinary jobs
segments.summary: At $66 a week they earned double the Savoy's pay and triple a laborer's, plus hundred dollars doubling in theatres.

segments.title: The first film money and the rumoured Bing and Cab clash
segments.summary: They made so much on The Big Broadcast of 1934 that pay arrangements changed; Hinton asks about friction between Bing and Cab.

segments.title: Bing Crosby at the Paramount and the film scale
segments.summary: Thomas recalls Bing as extra attraction, Russ Columbo's rivalry, and film pay of ten dollars an hour thanks to Mills.

segments.title: Smitty out, Al Morgan in: the string bass arrives
segments.summary: The band updates after Duke by replacing tuba player Smitty with string bassist Al Morgan.

segments.title: Benny Payne's joining date, from a phone call
segments.summary: They phone Payne, who recalls joining on November 21, 1931 at the Audubon when billing became Cab Calloway and His Orchestra.

segments.title: Straw boss and the notice rescinded by Mills
segments.summary: Thomas explains how he got his notice and Mills ordered it rescinded.

segments.title: Genealogy of new members: trombones, trumpets and Swayzee
segments.summary: Looking at the photo, they work out who replaced R.Q. Dickerson, and what became of Swayzee.

segments.title: Subbing for Johnny Hodges one night with Duke Ellington
segments.summary: Thomas played the parts for Hodges at a Fifth Avenue club beside Harry Carney, and Hinton recalls his own night with Duke.

segments.title: Closing the Part 3 interview
segments.summary: Hinton suggests another session on Duke.
